(Ln. 418-419): “We selected days seven and 60 for isotope labeling based on results from the parallel 220-day incubation, allowing us to capture differences between relatively fast and slow phases of microbial activity.”
3. The 18O-H2O labeling might introduce errors through abiotic pathways, like the oxygen exchange between water molecules and organic matter. But the authors didn't verify the specificity of the labeling. For instance, it is not determined whether the labeling only reflects microbial activity.
Authors’ response: We agree there might be errors via abiotic pathways with the 18O-H2O label, which is why we had included both abiotic and biotic treatments using either 18O-H2O or natural abundance H2O (Fig. S1). Using these treatments, we were able to directly compare assigned formula to identify which peaks were biotic-specific that picked up the label. We have clarified this within the main text to direct the reader to this method.
Authors’ changes: (Ln. 465-475): “Formula with enriched incorporation of isotope 18O were determined by direct comparison of biotic and abiotic samples from both samples that were exposed to 18O-H O and those that had a natural abundance (termed “16O-H O”) water pulse.
Isotopic Pattern Algorithm (IPA) implemented in Formularity software was used to detect 18O and other isotopologue peaks of formula detected in 18O-enriched and -unenriched H O samples.
Abundance ratios (AR) of 18O isotopologue and monoisotopic peaks in 18O-enriched and -unenriched H O samples were used to determine the 18O enrichment in identified formula. In cases when an 18O isotopologue peak was not detected in H O samples with natural abundance 18O enrichment, AR was calculated from the simulation by ecipex software49. 4. The filtering criteria for characteristic peaks of FT-ICR-MS and LC-MS/MS, such as a signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) of 2 and peak intensity thresholds, are too lenient. This may lead to the introduction of false positive peaks, resulting in calculation errors in molecular diversity. For example, the molecular diversity of the 18O-labeled peaks in Figure 3 may include instrumental noise.
Authors’ response: We have updated the methods section to clarify that both the 21T FTICR and 7T were used, with different s/n ratios. It is also unlikely that these selected peak filters introduced false peaks or instrument noise in FT-ICR-MS measurements. Described 21T FT-ICR instrument uses FT acquisition computer from an LTQ-FT Ultra (ThermoFisher Scientific, San Jose, CA, USA) (Ipsen, 2014). Peaks were extracted using Thermo Xcalibur 2.2 ((ThermoFisher Scientific, San Jose, CA, USA) libraries with calculated “S/N” of 2 based on direct ratio of peak intensity and instrument recorded noise information. Although we do not routinely record time domain transient signal, in our previous tests and estimates, on this instrument, cut-off of 2 would correspond to standard signal processing S/N of more than 7σ. Xcalibur software also automatically removed artifact harmonic peaks.
Ipsen, A. Efficient Calculation of Exact Fine Structure Isotope Patterns via the Multidimensional Fourier Transform. Anal Chem 86, 5316–5322 (2014).

Putatively identified molecules for each metabolite feature, based on MS/MS similarity [Global Natural Products Social Molecular Networking (GNPS) top--hit] as unique chemical “species”, were used to track changes in DOM composition as well as quantify molecular richness and diversity for eight time points from the incubation (days 1, 2, 8, 32, 60, 100, 140, and 220)16. DOM molecular richness, molecular diversity (Hill Numbers when q=2; annotated as HN ), and DOM functional molecular (q=2) diversity (multivariate Rao quadratic entropy; annotated as Rao ) indices were (multivariate) calculated from these features by converting peak heights to relative abundance across samples12,13.
To explore in greater detail how microbial products influence changes in DOM molecular diversity, we leveraged 18O-labeled H O as an isotopic tracer with Fourier Transform Ion 2 Cyclotron Resonance Mass Spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS) at two different decomposition time points: day seven and day 60 (Fig. S1). 18O-H O is taken up by actively growing microorganisms 2 and incorporated into their biomolecules (e.g., nucleic acids and lipids), but it is also used in numerous other pathways including enzymatic reactions during metabolism17–19. Prior 18O-H O 2 tracing experiments have primarily tracked microbial growth and carbon use efficiency using stable isotope probing and Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometry (IRMS)18,19, however to our knowledge previous experiments have not attempted to use 18O-H O as an isotopic tracer to 2 track microbial driven DOM composition transformations with mass spectrometry.
To determine microbial products during very early and later stages (seven and 60 days) of decomposition we pulsed labeled microcosms of plant litter and a soil microbial community with 18O-H O. DOM from water (polar, hydrophilic compounds), chloroform (non-polar, hydrophobic 2 compounds) and methanol (moderately polar compounds) extractions20 were analyzed using FT-ICR-MS to identify compounds isotopically enriched with 18O. To determine the efficiency of the isotope uptake by microorganisms we analyzed the water and chloroform extractable organic matter using IRMS to quantify δ18O. To further identify changes in metabolite abundances we used gas chromatography mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and to quantify molecular richness, abundance-based molecular diversity (HN ) and functional molecular diversity (q=2) (Rao ) of DOM, we used LC-MS/MS data.”
